summary: How often indicators are read: the length of a period and when the cycle's year starts.
definition: How often something is reported, and when each round is due: the length of one period in months, the month the cycle's year starts, and how many days after a period closes the report is due. A KPI names one, and the periods its readings are recorded for are derived from it, never stored again; a period is named by the month it ends. One cycle is shared by every measure read on that rhythm. A reporting cycle is not a data source's refresh (how often the numbers in the source change), not a horizon (the span an aim covers), and not a single report or its audience.

/spec/periodMonths.guide: How many months one period covers: 1, 3, 6 or 12. Choose the rhythm the sources can actually supply.

poor.text: 1, for measures read from forms transcribed once a season
poor.why: Two months in three would have nothing to read; the period is as short as the source allows, no shorter.

/spec/startMonth.guide: The month of the year the first period opens, from 1 to 12. Periods are laid out from it, so it decides which month each period ends in.
good: 9, for a cooperative whose season year opens in September

poor.text: 1, for a seasonal cycle when the season year opens in September
poor.why: Periods would end in March, June, September and December, cutting across the seasons the readings describe.

/spec/dueOffsetDays.guide: How many days after a period closes the report is due, allowing for the time the figures take to arrive.
good: 14, for a seasonal cycle whose forms are transcribed in the two weeks after the season

poor.text: 0, when the figures take weeks to transcribe
poor.why: Every round would be late on the day it closes.

/metadata/name.guide: The name, as people say it and as lists show it.

KPI:/spec/cycle.ask: Which KPIs are read on this cycle?
KPI:/spec/cycle.ifNone: Nothing has to be defined first: a cycle stands on its own, and a KPI names it when its means of verification are set.
